title: DOES “HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER” MEAN YOU MUST ENDURE THEIR ABUSE? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHRISTIANS WERE NEVER TAUGHT
paragraphs: DOES “HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER” MEAN YOU MUST ENDURE THEIR ABUSE? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHRISTIANS WERE NEVER TAUGHT

When the people who were supposed to protect you became the reason you needed healing, does God really expect you to keep suffering in the name of obedience? What Scripture actually says about honoring parents, confronting abuse, setting boundaries, forgiveness, and the Jesus who never confuses holiness with helplessness.
There is a kind of pain that becomes even harder to carry when someone opens a Bible and uses it against you.
Imagine a grown daughter sitting in her car outside her childhood home.
Her hands are shaking. Her chest feels tight. She has been staring at her phone for almost twenty minutes.
Her mother has called seven times.
The messages are getting worse.
“You are ungrateful.”
“After everything I've sacrificed for you.”
“God will punish you for dishonoring your mother.”
And then comes the verse she has heard since she was a little girl.
“Honor thy father and thy mother.”
She knows the commandment. She believes the Bible. She loves Jesus.
But she also remembers the screaming. The humiliation. The threats. The years of being told that her feelings were rebellion and her silence was righteousness.
She remembers apologizing for things she never did just to make the shouting stop.
She remembers being afraid to tell anyone what happened behind closed doors because, after all, they were a Christian family.
And now, as an adult, she is asking a question that makes her feel almost ashamed.
“If I stop allowing my parents to hurt me, am I disobeying God?”
Perhaps that daughter is you.
Perhaps you are a son who grew up believing that being a good Christian meant never questioning your father's cruelty.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to earn affection from a parent who only knows how to control you through guilt, fear, money, or Scripture.
Or perhaps you are reading this while raising your own children, terrified that the wounds you inherited might someday become wounds you pass down.
Whatever brought you here, please hear this before we open another passage.
God did command you to honor your parents. He did not command your parents to abuse you.
And those are two profoundly different things.
Because sometimes the deepest spiritual confusion begins when someone takes a holy commandment and uses it to protect unholy behavior.
The Bible must never become a weapon that silences the wounded while protecting the person inflicting the wounds.
And if we are going to understand what God actually requires, we cannot begin with family traditions, cultural expectations, or the opinions of people who have never lived through what you survived.
We must begin with Scripture.
In Exodus 20:12, God declares:
“Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.” (KJV)
The original Hebrew begins:
כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ
Kabbēd ʾet-ʾāvīkha veʾet-ʾimmekha.
“Honor your father and your mother.”
The Hebrew verb כַּבֵּד (kabbēd) comes from the root כבד (k-b-d), associated with weight, heaviness, and importance.
In this commandment, it conveys treating one's parents as worthy of honor, giving their relationship and responsibilities appropriate seriousness rather than treating them with contempt.
It is not a Hebrew word meaning “allow yourself to be destroyed.”
It does not mean “submit to every demand, regardless of its morality.”
And it does not mean “pretend evil is good because the person committing it gave you life.”
The commandment is real. It is holy. It remains morally significant.
But its meaning must be understood alongside everything else God has revealed.
That is where many wounded Christians have been failed.
They were taught one commandment without being taught the other Scriptures that protect its proper meaning.
They heard “Honor your parents” repeatedly.
But they rarely heard what God says directly to parents.
Ephesians 6:1–4 begins:

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth.”
Then Paul continues:
“And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.” (KJV)
Did you notice something?
The passage does not give parents unlimited authority.
It places responsibilities upon them.
The same chapter that commands children to obey also warns fathers against mistreating their children.
In the Greek text, Paul writes:
Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν
Kai hoi pateres, mē parorgizete ta tekna hymōn.
“And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger.”
The verb παροργίζετε (parorgizete) refers to provoking or arousing anger.
It is not a technical Greek term for every form of abuse. We should not pretend that it is.
But Paul's command clearly establishes that parental authority is not beyond moral accountability.
Parents are not given permission to exercise authority in ways that embitter, crush, or spiritually damage their children.
Colossians 3:21 makes the concern even clearer:
“Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.” (KJV)
That final warning matters.
Lest they be discouraged.
God sees what destructive treatment can do to a child's spirit.
He is not indifferent when a child becomes afraid to speak.
He is not indifferent when constant humiliation slowly replaces confidence with shame.
He is not indifferent when the very people entrusted with nurturing a child's life become sources of terror.
The Bible commands honor.
But it also commands parents to exercise their responsibilities without provoking and discouraging their children.
Both truths belong in the same conversation.
And neither can be erased to make the other more convenient.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
What happens when parental authority demands something contrary to God's will?
In Acts 5:29, Peter and the apostles declare:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” (KJV)
The immediate context concerns the apostles being ordered by religious authorities to stop proclaiming Jesus. It is not specifically a passage about abusive parents.
Nevertheless, it expresses a fundamental biblical principle: human authority is subordinate to God.
No parent possesses the authority to command sin.
No parent has divine permission to force a child into wrongdoing.
No family relationship can make cruelty righteous.
And no human authority becomes absolute merely because someone attaches God's name to it.
Even Ephesians 6:1 qualifies obedience with the words “in the Lord.”
The Greek phrase is:
ἐν κυρίῳ — en kyriō
“In the Lord.”
Christ remains the ultimate authority.
This does not mean every parental disagreement becomes a reason for disobedience. It does not erase a child's ordinary responsibility to obey appropriate parental guidance.
But it does mean that obedience to parents must never be turned into a rival to obedience to Christ.
And there is an important distinction that Christians must understand.
Honor and obedience are related, but they are not identical.
A young child ordinarily owes appropriate obedience to parental direction within a parent's legitimate authority.
An adult child continues to owe honor, but adulthood does not create a lifelong obligation to obey every parental instruction.
Honoring an aging parent might mean ensuring that they have necessary care, speaking truthfully without needless contempt, or refusing to exploit their vulnerability.
It does not necessarily mean giving them unrestricted access to your home, finances, marriage, children, private information, or emotional life.
You can acknowledge the significance of the relationship without agreeing to harmful demands.
You can refuse to retaliate without pretending nothing happened.
You can speak respectfully while firmly saying no.
And sometimes, when serious abuse is involved, you may need to create substantial distance or end direct contact to protect yourself or others.
Those decisions deserve wisdom, prayer, and, when possible, guidance from people who understand abuse and take safety seriously.
But distance is not automatically dishonor.
And access is not automatically love.
Imagine someone repeatedly entering your home and setting fires.
You would not prove your forgiveness by handing them another match.
You would put out the fire.
You would protect the people inside.
You would stop allowing the destruction.
And if the person genuinely repented, you would still have to consider what accountability, safety, and restored trust would require.
Why, then, do some Christians treat emotional, physical, sexual, or spiritual abuse as though it becomes less serious when the person responsible is a parent?
Why do we sometimes demand more endurance from the wounded than repentance from the one who caused the wounds?
Why does the victim hear sermons about forgiveness while the person who refuses to change hears almost nothing about accountability?
That is not a small pastoral problem.
It can become a serious distortion of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come to make evil comfortable.
He came to save sinners, expose darkness, and reconcile people to God through His death and resurrection.
And His grace never requires us to rename evil as goodness.
Listen to the words of Jesus in Luke 17:3:
“Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.” (KJV)
Notice that Jesus does not tell His followers to pretend the trespass never happened.
He speaks of confronting wrongdoing.
He speaks of repentance.
He speaks of forgiveness.
These are morally serious realities.
Forgiveness is not the same thing as denial.
And reconciliation is not the same thing as forgiveness.
You may choose to release vengeance and entrust justice to God while still recognizing that someone is not safe to be around.
You may pray for a parent's repentance without immediately restoring access.
You may desire their salvation without trusting their promises.
You may forgive and still need time to heal.
You may forgive and still tell the truth about a crime.
You may forgive and still seek protection from the authorities.
Forgiveness does not turn an unsafe person into a safe person. Repentance must be more than a sentence spoken after consequences arrive.
And Scripture gives us a vivid picture of this distinction.
Consider David and King Saul.
Saul was the king of Israel, a man holding real authority over David.
Yet Saul repeatedly sought David's life.
David did not conclude that honoring God's anointed king required standing still while Saul killed him.
He fled.
He took refuge.
He refused to murder Saul in revenge when opportunities arose.
In 1 Samuel 24 and 26, David demonstrated restraint while maintaining the distance necessary to survive.
David's situation was not a parent-child relationship, and we should not force the story to say something it was not written to say.
But it illustrates an important principle.
Respect for an authority figure and refusal to retaliate do not necessarily require remaining within reach of that person's violence.
David could refuse vengeance without surrendering his life.
That distinction matters.
Especially to the person who has been told that walking away is hatred.
Sometimes walking away is simply refusing to participate in further destruction.
And then there is Joseph.
A young man betrayed by his own brothers.
Sold into slavery.
Separated from his father.
Robbed of years he could never recover.
Imagine the confusion.
The fear.
The loneliness.
The questions he must have carried.
What did I do to deserve this?
Why would my own family do this?
Where was God when they sold me?
Years later, when Joseph encountered his brothers again, he possessed the power to retaliate.
But he did not.
In Genesis 50:20, Joseph said:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” (KJV)
Read that carefully.
Joseph did not say that his brothers' actions were good.
He said they meant evil.
Evil.
He did not rewrite their intentions to make his testimony sound more spiritual.
He acknowledged their wrongdoing while recognizing God's providence.
That is an extraordinary distinction.
God's ability to bring redemption out of evil does not make the evil righteous.
And the fact that God can use your suffering does not mean He approved of the person who inflicted it.
Joseph's story also shows that restoration involved a process. He observed his brothers' conduct and responses before fully revealing himself and embracing them.
The story does not establish a universal formula for every family relationship. But it certainly does not teach that trust must be restored blindly or immediately.
And perhaps that is something you need to hear.
God can redeem what happened to you without asking you to call what happened good.
You do not have to describe abuse as discipline when it was cruelty.
You do not have to describe manipulation as concern when it was control.
You do not have to describe threats as spiritual correction when they were intimidation.
You do not have to pretend that the wound was imaginary simply because the person who caused it refuses to acknowledge it.
The truth matters to God.
Proverbs 12:22 says:
“Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.” (KJV)
Truthfulness is not dishonor.
Speaking honestly about abuse is not inherently rebellion.
Seeking help is not betrayal.
And protecting a vulnerable child from someone who has harmed them is not a failure to honor the family.
It is a serious responsibility.
Now, there is another passage we must face, because someone will inevitably bring it up.
Matthew 15:4 records Jesus saying:
“For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.” (KJV)
Some people read that and become terrified.
They assume that any refusal, disagreement, or boundary is equivalent to cursing their parents.
But that is not what the passage teaches.
Jesus was confronting religious leaders who had used their traditions to avoid the obligation to care for their parents.
He was defending God's command against religious hypocrisy.

The command concerning cursing parents comes from the Mosaic law's treatment of serious offenses. It cannot responsibly be reduced to “Any adult child who says no to an abusive parent is under God's condemnation.”
Nor does it authorize Christians to impose the ancient Israelite civil penalty.
Jesus was exposing people who used religion to escape genuine obligations.
He was not commanding victims to submit to abuse.
And when we read the Gospels more broadly, we discover something remarkable about how Jesus related to family loyalty.
In Matthew 10:37, He said:
“He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” (KJV)
Jesus did not teach contempt for parents.
He cared for His own mother even while suffering on the cross, entrusting her to the beloved disciple in John 19:26–27.
But He also made something unmistakably clear.
Family relationships, however precious, must never occupy the place that belongs to God.
A parent's voice is not the voice of Christ simply because that parent claims to speak for Him.
And when a family member demands loyalty at the expense of truth, righteousness, or safety, that demand must be evaluated under the authority of Jesus.
Not under fear.
Not under manipulation.
Not under the threat that God will stop loving you if you refuse to comply.
Because the Gospel is not a system in which a frightened child must earn God's acceptance by keeping an abusive adult happy.
The Gospel announces that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Your salvation is not purchased by perfect compliance with every family expectation.
It is God's gift through faith in Christ.
And if you belong to Christ, your identity is not ultimately defined by the cruelest thing someone called you.
Not “worthless.”
Not “ungrateful.”
Not “a disappointment.”
Not “impossible to love.”
Not “a curse upon this family.”
Those labels may have echoed through your childhood.
But they are not the Gospel.
In Christ, believers are adopted into God's family.
Romans 8:15 speaks of receiving “the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.” (KJV)
The Greek text preserves the Aramaic address:
Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ — Abba ho Patēr
“Abba, Father.”
Abba is an Aramaic word for father, carried into the Greek text alongside Patēr, the Greek word for father.
It communicates a real familial address to God, not a magical word and not merely a childish nickname.
And for someone whose earthly father made the word “father” feel frightening, this passage may be both beautiful and difficult.
Perhaps you struggle to imagine fatherly love without conditions.
Perhaps the word itself brings memories you wish you could forget.
If that is you, you do not have to pretend that trust comes easily.
The character of God is not defined by the failures of your earthly parents.
God is not a larger version of the person who terrified you.
His holiness is not cruelty.
His authority is not manipulation.
His correction is not sadism.
His love is not a trap.
Psalm 27:10 says:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” (KJV)
That verse does not promise that every painful family relationship will be repaired in this lifetime.
But it does testify that abandonment by earthly parents does not place someone beyond God's care.
And maybe you have been carrying a question for years.
“If my own parents could not love me well, why would God?”
Look at Jesus.
Look at the One who welcomed the vulnerable.
Look at the One who warned against causing little ones to stumble.
Look at the One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
Look at the One who suffered injustice without becoming unjust.
Look at the cross, where God's love and holiness are revealed in the saving work of His Son.
Jesus was not crucified to preserve the reputation of abusive families.
He died for sinners and rose again, so that all who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
That includes wounded children who have grown into exhausted adults.
And it also includes parents who have committed terrible wrongs, if they genuinely turn to Christ.
But we must be careful here.
The possibility of redemption does not eliminate accountability.
A parent who has abused a child cannot demand immediate trust simply because they say, “God forgave me.”
A confession may be a beginning.
It is not a substitute for changed behavior.
True repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist said in Matthew 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” (KJV)
The Greek expression καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας (karpon axion tēs metanoias) speaks of fruit appropriate to repentance.
Repentance is not merely sorrow at being exposed.
It involves a genuine turning away from sin.

For an abusive parent, that may include acknowledging specific wrongdoing without excuses, stopping harmful conduct, accepting appropriate consequences, seeking qualified help, making restitution where possible, and respecting the boundaries of those harmed.
It may involve cooperating with lawful investigations.
It may involve accepting that the relationship will never return to what it once was.
And it certainly does not entitle the person who caused harm to control the healing process of the person they wounded.
Grace is free.
Trust is not automatic.
Forgiveness is commanded as part of Christian life, but restored access is not owed on demand.
And even when reconciliation is possible, it must not come at the expense of safety or truth.
Perhaps you are reading this and feeling guilty because you have not spoken to a parent in months.
Maybe years.
You see Mother's Day posts.
Father's Day celebrations.
Photographs of families laughing around dinner tables.
And something inside you aches.
You wonder why you cannot have what everyone else seems to have.
You wonder whether you should call.
You wonder whether your boundaries are too harsh.
You wonder whether God is disappointed.
And sometimes, the hardest part is that you still love them.
You miss the parent you needed.
You remember the good moments.
The birthday cake.
The occasional embrace.
The rare words of encouragement.
The times they seemed almost like the parent you had prayed for.
And that makes everything more confusing.
Because abuse does not always erase affection.
Sometimes affection and fear become tangled together so tightly that a person no longer knows what healthy love feels like.
You can grieve someone who is still alive.
You can love a parent and recognize that being near them is harmful.
You can wish for reconciliation and acknowledge that reconciliation is not currently possible.
You can remember moments of kindness without allowing those moments to erase patterns of abuse.
The existence of good memories does not cancel the reality of serious harm.
And protecting yourself does not mean you have stopped caring.
For some people, healthy boundaries may look like limiting phone calls.
For others, refusing conversations that become threatening or degrading.
For others, declining financial demands or preventing a parent from using children as instruments of control.
For some, contact may need to happen only through a trusted intermediary.
And for others, especially where serious danger, coercion, or repeated abuse is involved, no contact may be necessary.
The Bible does not give one universal contact schedule for every adult child and every abusive parent.
Wisdom requires attention to the actual situation.
Proverbs 22:3 says:
“A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.” (KJV)
The proverb commends prudence in the face of danger.
It should not be treated as a simplistic command to sever every difficult relationship.
But neither should Christians dismiss the wisdom of taking protective action when harm is foreseeable.
And if you are a minor experiencing abuse, the burden should not fall on you to negotiate the situation alone.
Tell a trustworthy adult who can help protect you, such as a safe relative, teacher, counselor, safeguarding officer, or appropriate authority.
If you are in immediate danger, seek emergency assistance.
If sexual abuse, serious violence, or threats are involved, seeking protection and reporting to appropriate authorities can be necessary.
Please do not interpret any teaching about forgiveness as a reason to remain in immediate danger.
A church should never pressure someone to conceal abuse for the sake of its reputation.
The reputation of Christ is not protected by hiding wickedness.
It is honored by truth, justice, compassion, and integrity.
And now I want to speak to a different person.
The parent reading this who is beginning to feel uncomfortable.
Perhaps your adult child has pulled away.
Perhaps they no longer answer every call.
Perhaps they have told you that certain words or behaviors hurt them.
And your first reaction has been anger.
“How dare they?”
“I raised them.”
“I paid for everything.”
“They owe me respect.”
But what if, instead of beginning with what they owe you, you asked what your conduct has taught them to expect from you?
What if their silence is not necessarily arrogance?
What if their distance is not necessarily hatred?
What if they have tried to explain their pain, and every attempt became another argument they could not win?
Not every accusation is accurate.
Not every disagreement is abuse.
Parents can be unfairly blamed, and children can behave wrongly too.
But a parent's authority is never a reason to dismiss a serious allegation without examination.
If your child says they were harmed, listen carefully.
Do not begin by defending your intentions.
Ask whether your actions were wrong.
Ask whether you have used fear, humiliation, intimidation, or Scripture to maintain control.
Ask whether your apologies have required your child to comfort you instead of allowing them to speak.
Ask whether you have confused obedience with love.
And if you discover that you have sinned against your child, repent.
Not theatrically.
Not as a strategy to regain access.
Not by saying, “I'm sorry you feel that way.”
Repent with humility.
Tell the truth.
Take responsibility.
Seek help.
Accept consequences.
And do not demand that your child's healing happen according to your timetable.
Because your child is not your property.
Your child is a human being made in the image of God.
Parenthood is a stewardship.
It is not ownership.
And the God who calls children to honor their parents also calls parents to answer for how they treat their children.
There is still grace for the repentant parent.
There is still mercy at the cross.
There is still the possibility of transformation through Jesus Christ.
But grace does not make confession unnecessary.
It makes genuine repentance possible.
And now, perhaps, we are reaching the deepest part of this conversation.
Because for many wounded Christians, the question is no longer simply, “Must I endure abuse?”
The question beneath it is:
“Can I belong to Jesus without betraying myself?”
Can I tell the truth?
Can I protect my children?
Can I stop pretending?
Can I acknowledge that my childhood was not what it should have been?
Can I grieve the mother who was physically present but emotionally absent?
Can I mourn the father whose approval I spent my entire life trying to earn?
Can I admit that I am angry?
Can I bring that anger before God without pretending to be spiritually mature?
The Psalms give us a language for anguish.
They contain tears, protest, lament, fear, and desperate cries for help.
Biblical faith is not the absence of pain.
It is bringing our pain into the presence of the God who hears.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
That does not mean every emotional wound disappears immediately after prayer.
Healing can take time.
Some people need trauma-informed counseling, medical care, pastoral support, practical protection, and patient community.
Seeking that help does not demonstrate a lack of faith.
It can be part of wise and faithful stewardship of the life God has given you.
And please remember this.
You do not have to become emotionally numb to prove that you have forgiven.
You do not have to stop grieving to prove that you trust God.
You do not have to rush reconciliation to prove that you are a Christian.
You do not have to turn every painful memory into a testimony before you are ready to speak about it.
There is a difference between surrendering bitterness to God and suppressing the truth of what happened.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
The command is against personal vengeance.
It is not a command to abandon lawful protection, accountability, or justice.
You can refuse revenge while seeking justice.
You can pray for someone while maintaining distance.
You can desire their repentance without exposing yourself to another cycle of harm.
And you can entrust what you cannot control to God.
This is not easy.
Sometimes obedience to Jesus requires courage that nobody sees.
The courage to say, “I will not lie about what happened.”
The courage to say, “I cannot allow you to speak to me this way.”
The courage to say, “My children will not be exposed to the same danger.”
The courage to say, “I hope you repent, but I cannot pretend that trust has been restored.”
The courage to say, “I am willing to seek peace, but I cannot manufacture reconciliation alone.”
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” (KJV)
Those words matter.
“If it be possible.”
“As much as lieth in you.”
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always within one person's power.
You are responsible for your conduct.
You are not able to control another person's repentance.
You cannot create mutual trust by yourself.
You cannot make someone safe simply by loving them harder.
And you cannot carry both sides of a relationship indefinitely while calling the exhaustion holiness.
That may be the sentence someone needs to hear today.
Because you have tried.
You have explained.
You have cried.
You have apologized.
You have prayed.
You have gone back again and again, hoping that this time the conversation would be different.
And perhaps it never was.
If that is your story, I will not promise that your parent will change.
I will not promise that the next phone call will bring an apology.
I will not promise that every family relationship will be restored before heaven.
The Bible does not give us permission to make those guarantees.
But it gives us something greater than a false promise.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
The Savior who knows what rejection feels like.
The Savior who was betrayed.
The Savior who was falsely accused.
The Savior who suffered at the hands of sinful people.
And yet the Savior who did not surrender His righteousness to the evil surrounding Him.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Jesus understands suffering without approving of sin.
He understands betrayal without calling betrayal love.
He understands injustice without declaring injustice holy.
And through His resurrection, He has conquered sin and death.
That is why the Christian hope is more than learning to manage painful relationships.
It is the promise of redemption through Christ.
The Gospel does not say your wounds are insignificant.
It says your wounds do not have the final authority over your life.
It does not say your past was acceptable.
It says your past does not have to become your eternal identity.
It does not say that everyone who harmed you will repent.
It says that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust, even when people have betrayed it.
And for the one who has spent years believing that love must always hurt, that truth may take time to receive.
But it is worth holding onto.
Because honoring your father and mother must never become an excuse for dishonoring the God whose image you bear.
You are not greater than your parents.
You are not called to despise them.
You are not authorized to return evil for evil.
But neither are you a disposable object whose suffering becomes righteous whenever a parent demands it.
You are a person accountable to God.
And so are they.
Maybe this article has exposed something you have never said out loud.
Maybe you have been using the word “honor” to justify staying in a destructive situation.
Maybe you have been using the word “forgiveness” to avoid admitting how deeply you were wounded.
Maybe you have spent years protecting your family's public image while privately wondering why your soul feels exhausted.
Or perhaps you are a parent who now realizes that you have used a commandment meant to cultivate honor as a tool for demanding unquestioning control.
Wherever you find yourself, the invitation of Jesus is not to hide.
It is to come into the light.
To repent where you have sinned.
To seek help where you have been harmed.
To forgive without lying.
To pursue peace without surrendering truth.
To practice honor without enabling evil.
And to trust that the grace of God is powerful enough to transform lives without requiring us to deny reality.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior matters.
Not because we have every answer.
Not because every wound can be healed through a single article.
But because people desperately need to encounter the whole counsel of Scripture, centered on Jesus Christ, rather than isolated verses used to manipulate the vulnerable.
Some people need to hear about repentance.
Others need to hear that God's grace is not beyond their reach.
Some need the courage to confess.
Others need the courage to seek protection.
Some need to forgive.
Others need to understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are not interchangeable.
And all of us need Jesus.
Not merely to increase the reach of a post, but because someone in your circle may be silently asking the same question.
Someone who has never told anyone why they dread going home.
Someone who thinks setting a boundary will send them to hell.
Someone who has confused parental authority with divine authority.
Someone who needs to know that God does not require them to conceal abuse.
Where someone's safety or privacy could be affected, send the article privately rather than publicly identifying them as a survivor.
There may come a day when guilt returns and you need to read these Scriptures again.
Not the details of trauma you are not ready to share.
Not anything that could compromise your safety.
Just one honest response.

If you have a testimony of repentance, restored relationships, healthy boundaries, or God's faithfulness through a difficult family situation, your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.

And if you disagree with something in this article, you are welcome to engage respectfully with Scripture. We should be willing to examine our understanding carefully, because truth matters more than winning an argument.
There is also something deeper I want to invite you into.
Not because a payment can purchase His favor.
Not because giving to this particular ministry is a condition of obedience or salvation.
It is not.
But because voluntary, faithful generosity can help make Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers should give willingly rather than under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
If you already support your local church, care for your family, or have financial obligations that must come first, please honor those responsibilities.
It can help turn the message you just read into an ongoing mission.
Because the greatest gift of the Gospel cannot be bought.
And it cannot be sold.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep sharing truth.
And keep following Jesus.
Because there are people suffering behind closed doors who do not need another verse used against them.
They need the truth of Scripture rightly understood.
They need safe people who will listen.
They need repentance where there has been wrongdoing.
They need wisdom about boundaries.
They need the hope of redemption.
And above all, they need Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, I want to return to that daughter sitting in her car.
The phone is still on the seat beside her.
The messages have not disappeared.
Her childhood has not suddenly become beautiful.
Her mother has not necessarily repented.
Nothing about the past has been magically undone.
But perhaps something has changed.
For the first time, she is beginning to understand that she does not have to answer every threatening message to prove she loves God.
She can pray.
She can seek wise counsel.
She can take appropriate steps toward safety.
She can refuse cruelty without becoming cruel.
She can grieve what she never received.
She can leave room for genuine repentance without pretending that repentance has already happened.
And she can follow Jesus without surrendering her conscience to another person's control.
Maybe she places the phone down.
Maybe she cries.
Maybe she whispers a prayer she has been too afraid to pray.

“Lord Jesus, help me know what is right. Keep me from hatred. Give me courage to tell the truth. Teach me to forgive without enabling sin. Protect those who are vulnerable. And please heal what I cannot heal on my own.”
It is not a dramatic speech.
It does not solve everything.
But it is honest.
And sometimes honesty before God is where a new chapter begins.
If you recognize yourself in her story, remember that the Savior who calls you to honor your parents also calls you to walk in truth.
He is not asking you to worship your family.
He is asking you to follow Him.
And His grace is sufficient to meet you even in the complicated, unfinished places of your life.
You may never receive the apology your childhood deserved, but the cross declares that your future does not have to remain imprisoned by the sins of your past.
